http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/14/us-ba.text: The United States has backed Japan's sovereignty over four islands controlled by Russia after Vladimir Putin became the first Russian president in 15 years to visit the disputed territory, prompting Tokyo to summon Moscow's ambassador and describe the trip as "absolutely unacceptable.""The United States remains unwavering in its support of its most important ally and in its recognition of Japanese sovereignty over the Northern Territories," the US ambassador to Tokyo George Glass said on X."At a time when the US-Japan alliance is dedicated to cultivating prosperity across the Indo-Pacific, we strongly oppose any action that undermines its peace and stability," Glass added.Russian-Japanese relations have long been dogged by the four southernmost islands in a volcanic chain off the coast of Hokkaido seized by the Soviet Union following an invasion in August 1945, in the final days of World War II.Moscow broke its formal neutrality with Japan just days before the invasion.The Japanese government maintains that the four islands and groups of islets that make up the Northern Territories — Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and Habomai — are part of its territory that the Soviets illegally occupied and Russia has continued to occupy since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.The dispute has kept the two countries from signing a peace treaty that would formally end their hostilities. They terminated the state of war in 1956.Moscow has reinforced its military presence on the islands as recently as December 2021, when it deployed Bastion coastal defence missile systems on an uninhabited volcanic island in the middle of the chain.The island hosted a Japanese army base prior to the Soviet occupation. A Soviet base there was shut down amid funding shortages in the wake of the collapse of the Soviet Union.Moscow previously deployed Bal and Bastion missile systems on two of the four southernmost islands in 2016.In the following years, Moscow further beefed up its arsenal on the islands by sending top-of-the-line air defence missile systems, setting up an air base on Etorofu Island, and deploying fighter jets.The sparsely inhabited islands are strategically significant to the Kremlin as they sit at the entrance to the Sea of Okhotsk and give Russia's Pacific Fleet access to the open Pacific without passing through Japanese-controlled waters.Putin's visit was the first by a Russian president since Dmitry Medvedev in 2010.'Absolutely unacceptable'Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters "the Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan's territory, both historically and under international law."Putin's visit "offends the sentiments of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable," she added.Japan's Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said his country “strongly protests” Putin's visit to the largest of the islands, Etorofu.“The Northern Territories, including Etorofu Island, are Japan’s inherent territory both historically and from the perspective of international law,” Motegi said in a statement.He summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to the ministry in Tokyo and lodged a strong protest over the visit, requesting that he "promptly report the message back to Moscow,” the minister told reporters afterwards.Russia's embassy in Japan said the ambassador reiterated Moscow's claim that the islands are part of Russia and that Putin's trip there was not "a matter for discussion with foreign states".The Kremlin boasted about the visit by posting a video of Putin on one of the four main islands. Russian state-run media said he had visited a fish-processing plant and showed him trying local caviar.Takaichi said the visit was a further blow to the already-strained ties between the two countries over Ukraine, and that Moscow should understand the consequences.Japan imposed sanctions on Russia after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.It also placed export controls on technology with military applications and provided financial support to Ukraine. Russia responded by designating Japan an "unfriendly state".Tokyo is now considering strengthening those sanctions as part of its countermeasures in response to Putin's trip.“We must say this visit has further hardened Japanese public sentiment toward Russia and has made it more difficult to restore bilateral relations in the medium to long term,” she said.“We hope the Russian side fully understands the seriousness of this.”

https://www.baltictimes.com/lithuania_sh.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Lithuania should not invest in airBaltic until airline turns profitable, president says 2026-08-21 LETA/BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - It would be irresponsible for Lithuania to invest in Latvia's loss-making national airline airBaltic until it returns to profitable operations, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said on Friday. "The company needs to make very radical decisions to reduce costs and increase its yield. Until such guarantees are in place, I believe it would be quite irresponsible to make any generous promises - while we do not see how the company's rise (...) from the ashes and its profitable activity will be ensured," Nauseda told reporters on Friday. According to the president, all financial aspects and risks must be evaluated before considering any acquisition of airBaltic shares. Nauseda noted that Lithuania remains interested in the success of the Latvian airline to ensure maximum flight connectivity during Lithuania's presidency of the European Union Council. "Let us not view the presidency solely as our officials' trips to Brussels and back. It is a very broad field of activity involving extensive travel, including to all EU members, the 26 state capitals besides Vilnius. There will be much activity, much travel, and for that reason, the convenience of transport is a very important aspect," Nauseda emphasised. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said in Riga on Wednesday that if Latvia made an offer, Lithuania would consider acquiring a stake in airBaltic, but only after assessing all arguments and prioritising its own interests. Earlier this week, Transport Minister Juras Taminskas said that if an offer to acquire shares were presented, he would not support it, calling it an "emotional action". The Latvian parliament on Thursday gave its preliminary approval to potential state participation in ensuring airBaltic's financial stability. This includes the acquisition of up to 30 million euros in interim financing bonds and the capitalisation of existing bonds worth 50 million euros. Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said this week that this was the last chance to save airBaltic. Comments Related Articles Subscribe Log In Ads Please enter your username and password. Close This week on the Hemp Show, we’re continuing our coverage of the National Industrial Hemp Council’s Global Industrial Hemp Fiber Summit, held at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York City during Fashion Week. It was two days of farmers, breeders, processors, machine builders, designers and brands, all focused on how to get hemp from the field into something somebody will buy. What it already is turns out to be a crop with farmers on one end, brands on the other, and a lot of empty space in between. Over two days, nearly every panel ran into that empty space from a different direction. So on this episode, we follow the missing middle and see what we know about how much we don’t know, and maybe some things we do know. Agriseeds kingsagriseeds.com Forever Green, distributors of the KP4 Hemp Cutter hempcutter.com The Lancaster Farming Industrial Hemp Podcast goes inside the 2026 NIHC Global Industrial Hemp Fiber Summit, held September 16 and 17 at the Fashion Institute of Technology (FIT) in New York City during Fashion Week. Host Eric Hurlock follows the summit's Seed to Style theme from start to finish, using sound bites from farmers, plant breeders, processors, machine builders, fiber scientists, textile brands and policy leaders. They all describe the same challenge: the "missing middle" of the industrial hemp supply chain. That's the processing, decortication, fiber standards, certified seed and buyer commitments needed to turn hemp stalks into yarn, fabric and finished products. National Industrial Hemp Council (NIHC) president Patrick Atagi opens the summit, and Paul Benhaim of The Hemp Plastic Company tells the room that "nobody on earth has a hemp budget." Day one covers hemp textiles from global sourcing to fiber science. Ryan Zaczynski of 1937 International describes a large hemp fiber project in Pakistan, led by Dr. Zafar Riaz and Dr. Nayyar Kazmi, with heat-tolerant genetics, water retting and a first commercial crop of about 4,000 acres expected in 2027. Ally Friedman of the Bezos Earth Fund explains why climate philanthropy is funding a hemp life-cycle assessment against cotton and polyester. Joe Hickey of the Kentucky Hemp Growers Co-op Association, Clyde Carpenter of the New York Fashion Innovation Center, University of Kentucky hemp economist Dr. Tyler Mark and Cornell University plant breeder Larry Smart cover fiber consistency, spinning mill requirements, crop rotation economics and domestic hemp seed. The day closes with hemp's sister fibers. Eric Singular of INCCert and the North American Linen Association makes the case for shared bast fiber processing for flax and hemp, and Buxton Midyette of Supima explains how USDA cotton classing, forensic fiber testing and supply chain traceability give mills confidence. Day two opens with Paul Benhaim's keynote on hemp fiber's value bottleneck, the brands missing from the room, and his call to "finance the middle." A USDA panel covers the ARS hemp germplasm repository in Geneva, New York, and AMS performance-based sampling for fiber hemp growers. The equipment panel, moderated by Trey Riddle of IND HEMP, features Lawrence Serbin's Fiber King green-hemp field decorticator, Guillaume Delannoy of FRD-CODEM on hemp fiber in automotive composites, Alex Teodorescu of Cretes on decortication technology, and Andrew Bish of the Hemp Feed Coalition on market pull. Jeremy Klettke of Davis Farms of Oregon explains counter-season hemp seed multiplication in Argentina. Ted Haney of the Federation of International Hemp Organizations explains why certified seed helped Canada build a commercial hemp industry. The episode also contrasts two textile supply chain models. Maciej Kowalski of Kombinat Konopny runs a vertically integrated hemp apparel chain in Poland, while Tim Almond of Heartland sells spin-ready hemp fiber to yarn mills, made to a published specification. On the materials panel, Cameron McIntosh of Americhanvre Cast Hemp talks about spray-applied hempcrete, and Greg Wilson of Hempwood talks about hemp flooring manufacturing costs. Winona LaDuke of the Indigenous Hemp Cooperative traces a Patagonia hemp bag through five states and two countries. Ira Vandever of Turquoise Indigo Fibers describes Indigenous standards for hemp and Navajo-Churro wool goods. Joseph Carringer of Canna Markets Group closes with a call to "let hemp be hemp" in fashion and textiles. It's essential listening for anyone following hemp fiber, hemp textiles, natural fibers, regional supply chains and the future of the U.S. industrial hemp industry.
